title: Milton Flats Rising
premise: Hazel Zhou, a piano tuner who reads a building's history through its radiators and pipes, is hired to prepare the condemned Milton Flats for its final inventory before demolition. Behind a tenant's old wardrobe she finds a box of undelivered letters from 1989, addressed to her own grandmother, implicating the family patriarch in a fire that displaced half the building. As Hazel traces the letters' recipients—now scattered, aging, some complicit—the demolition date becomes a deadline for a truth the family arranged itself around for thirty years. In the end, Hazel chooses truth over loyalty, reading the letters aloud at the family's farewell gathering in the empty lobby, and the family fractures but finally breathes.
about_author: D. M. Galloway is the pen name of a former building inspector turned writer who spent a decade documenting condemned housing projects across the Rust Belt. Their work has appeared in small literary journals, and 'Milton Flats Rising' is their first novel.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Hazel Zhou arrives at the condemned Milton Flats to tune the community center's dying upright piano, mapping the building's history through its radiators and water pipes. Her POV establishes her gift, her practiced smile that ends conversations, and her estrangement from the Zhou family. Emotional beat: wary competence masking loneliness as the demolition notice flaps on the door.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Clearing unit 4C, Hazel pries loose a wardrobe panel and finds a shoebox of forty-one letters, all stamped, none delivered, all addressed to Mei-Lin Zhou—her grandmother—in careful 1989 handwriting. POV shifts to Hazel's cousin Marcus, the family's loyal fixer, who urges her to burn them. Emotional beat: dread blooming under curiosity; the past has a pulse.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Kept
chapters.summary: Hazel visits Mei-Lin in her assisted-living apartment and shows her one letter. The old woman goes silent, then says only: 'Some houses fall down before the wrecking ball.' Hazel pieces together that the letters are from tenant Ruth Okafor, written after the 1989 stairwell fire. Emotional beat: the first crack in the family's polished surface; grief disguised as silence.

chapters.title: The Fire That Wasn't an Accident
chapters.summary: In alternating sections, Hazel researches county records while Marcus confronts their uncle Victor, the family patriarch, who admits he was the building's superintendent in 1989—and that he delivered nothing. The letters allege Victor ignored reported wiring faults to protect the owner, his brother-in-law. Emotional beat: loyalty begins to feel like complicity; Marcus wavers between protecting Victor and his own conscience.

chapters.title: Ruth Okafor's Address
chapters.summary: Hazel tracks Ruth's surviving daughter, Adaeze, now a retired nurse living across town, who remembers her mother writing until the day she died waiting for a reply that never came. Adaeze gives Hazel Ruth's journal. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: the abstract injury acquires a face and a voice; Hazel's smile fails her for the first time in years.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: At Sunday dinner, the family performs its usual choreography of avoidance, and Hazel realizes every seat, every topic change, was arranged around the fire's secret long before she was born. Victor privately offers to pay off the building's remaining tenants' claims quietly if Hazel hands over the box. Emotional beat: suffocating tenderness; love revealed as a system of silences.

chapters.title: Marcus's Ledger
chapters.summary: Marcus, who owes Victor his business loan and his reputation, secretly copies the letters and starts his own ledger of the family's debts—financial and moral. He discovers Victor has been paying a retired fire marshal for decades. POV: Marcus. Emotional beat: the loyalist turns double agent; guilt sharpens into resolve.

chapters.title: Nine Days
chapters.summary: With nine days until demolition, Victor escalates: he has the community center sealed early, cutting Hazel off from the piano and the building's voice. Hazel and Adaeze petition the city for a historical review, buying time but exposing the family to public scrutiny. Emotional beat: siege mentality; the house itself seems to resist its erasure.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: At the family's farewell gathering in the gutted lobby, Hazel breaks the arrangement: instead of a eulogy, she reads Ruth's letters aloud, ending with the journal's final line. Victor does not deny it; he simply sits down among the people he wronged. Marcus stands beside her. Emotional beat: cathartic rupture; truth spoken into a room built for forgetting.

chapters.title: Rising
chapters.summary: Demolition day. The family scatters and reforms in smaller, honest configurations—Victor funds restitution anonymously, Adaeze receives Ruth's undelivered words at last, and Hazel tunes a new piano in the rebuilt community center on the site. She no longer needs the smile that ends conversations. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope; what rises is not the building but the people.
